english.html: ly gazed, at the instant she was conceiving, upon a painting of a Moor that hung about her bed, produced a child black as an Ethiopian. St Jerome somewhere relates that an ugly woman, married to a hideous and deformed husband, having given birth to a handsome boy, was on that account greatly suspected and accused of adultery, and nevertheless saved by the counsel and prudence of that sovereign physician Hippocrates, who caused inquiry to be made whether in the woman's chamber there was some beautiful painting like the child; which was found, and thus the woman was delivered from the crime and the suspicion ſ. The books of the philosophers are full of it, that the things seen by the woman at the point of conception have great virtue to give form and imprint characters upon the creature that is engendered. Wherein all married people who take pleasure in paintings will take instruction not to keep in their chambers any that are ugly, monstrous or deformed, in order to avoid such scandals. On which no one (as I believe) knows not [unclear: the print reads nul ne ſçait, "no one knows"; the sense requires nul n'ignore] the history of Jacob, who, having agreed with Laban that every beast of the flocks speckled with any spots of diverse colour should be his for his wages, had green rods of diverse trees peeled and set in the watering-trough, together with the bark, so that the goats and ewes of the flock, looking upon the rods and the bark of differing colour, might likewise form their young speckled with unlike spots t. In the time of the Emperor Charles IV, some attest that a woman, for having gazed too fixedly, at the hour she was conceiving, upon an image of St John clothed in skins, gave birth to a daughter all hairy like a bear. Louis Vives, a man well lettered and versed in all disciplines, relates that Margaret, daughter of the Emperor Maximilian, in his time told a story to Jean Lamuze, a learned man and ambassador of King Ferdinand of Hungary: that in a town of Brabant which he names Buscunducis, as a general procession was being made in honour of some saint, and according to their old ceremonies some were dressed in the form of angels and others in the habit of devils, one of the latter, bounding and leaping through the streets all in
